content.title: CPI Inflation Report Today: Analysis of the March Core, Overall Data; What the Numbers Mean for Fed Rate Cuts
content.text: There was no doubt that the spike in gasoline prices was going to drive up price growth in March, but the latest data show the Iran war's effects on inflation were largely contained to energy, at least for now.That provided markets with a bit of good news to close out the week, but the U.S. is nowhere near the peak of inflation stemming from this latest Middle East conflict. The coming months could bring more headaches to both Federal Reserve officials and investors—and possibly diminish the market's hopes for lower interest rates later this year.The consumer price index rose 0.9% on the month in March, translating to a 3.3% year-over-year gain. That was largely in line with expectations, but still the highest level in nearly two years. It also represented a sizable jump from February's 0.3% monthly pace that saw headline inflation hit just 2.4% on an annual basis.Much of that was driven by a massive 21.2% monthly gain in gasoline prices that dragged the entire energy index up by 10.9%.Outside of the higher gas prices, Friday’s data didn’t show much evidence of broader effects of the Iran conflict. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, rose just 0.2% month over month, in line with February’s pace. Compared with a year ago, core inflation rose 2.6%, a touch below expectations.But while the core and headline prints were marginally softer than expected, the numbers were tempered by one-off price drops in March that likely won't continue.Prices for used cars and trucks, for example, fell 0.4% month over month in March, despite auto industry data showing the opposite.“Usually, the CPI gauge loosely tracks the used vehicle wholesale auction data with a lag of two to three months," writes Stephen Stanley, chief U.S. economist for Santander. "However, in the current instance, the auction data bottomed out in October and has increased by more than 6% cumulatively since then, which puts us now at least two months overdue for a rebound in the CPI measure of used vehicle prices."Additionally, the latest report showed that prices for prescription drugs, sporting event tickets, cable and streaming fees, and even health insurance all experienced major declines last month. Those readings, in some cases, are contrary, to what industry data and other price growth metrics have tracked—and again, are likely more one-off declines that investors shouldn’t count on to keep inflation reined in.Instead, economists largely believe that inflation will jump again in April. And that rise might not be based solely on elevated prices at the pump through the April survey period—costs were still $4.15 per gallon on average nationwide Friday. The March report did show some signs of broader-based inflationary effects from the ongoing Middle East conflict. Airfares, which tend to react quickly to fuel cost spikes, rose 2.7% in March. That could be a sign of things to come.Shelter prices might also prove to be a sticking point in the months ahead. Although housing inflation has been softer in recent months, that could be due more to data distortions carried over from the 2025 government shutdown. During that funding lapse, there was no CPI survey conducted in October, which meant that BLS staff penciled in a zero for October housing inflation. That data are part of the monthly calculations until April, when that subset of the housing panel is due to be surveyed. Economists expect that this distortion could lead to shelter costs accelerating somewhat in April.The latest numbers also don't seem to lessen the ongoing wedge between CPI inflation and the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, the personal consumption expenditures, or PCE, price index.Goldman Sachs and others noted Friday that based on the details in the CPI report, core PCE price index is expected to show a monthly increase of 0.22% in March, which corresponds to a year-over-year rate of 3.1%.Headline PCE inflation is expected to jump by 0.6% month over month for March, or an increase of about 3.4% from a year earlier. The Fed maintains a 2% inflation target.Looking ahead, it will be worth watching how Middle East supply-chain disruptions play out and whether they translate to upward pressure on areas outside of energy—including food, healthcare and input costs like metals.Meanwhile, higher tariffs do seem to be exerting some pressure on categories like apparel and home furnishings. Declining natural gas prices and slowing rents might help temper some of these pressures, but the early signs point to inflation remaining firm enough to close the door on Fed interest-rate cuts for much of the year.“Today's report complicates the Fed's calculus without fundamentally rewriting it,” writes Jason Pride, chief of investment strategy and research at Glenmede. “With the ceasefire still fragile and oil prices well above pre-war levels, the risk that inflation re-anchors above the 2% target is real.”
